title: Βοηλάτης καὶ Ἡρακλῆς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 72 (= Perry 291). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: An oxdriver was driving a wagon to a village.
sentences.n: Chambry prints this fable as verse, not prose — eight short lines in the choliambic metre of Babrius' verse Aesop, and the line breaks here are his. He also prints no moral for it: Heracles' own words are the moral.

sentences.t:
Τῆς δ’ ἐμπεσούσης εἰς φάραγγα κοιλώδη,
δέον βοηθεῖν, ὅδε ἀργὸς εἱστήκει,
τῷ δὲ Ἡρακλεῖ προσηύχετο μόνῳ
ἁπάντων θεῶν ὡς πολλὰ τιμωμένῳ.
sentences.tr:
Tēs d' empesousēs eis pharanga koilōdē,
deon boēthein, hode argos heistēkei,
tōi de Hēraklei prosēucheto monōi
hapantōn theōn hōs polla timōmenōi.
sentences.l: And it having fallen into a hollow ravine, though it was needful to help, this man stood idle, and prayed to Heracles alone of all the gods, as being greatly honoured by him.
sentences.i: When the wagon went down into a deep gully, and helping was what was needed, the fellow simply stood there doing nothing and prayed to Heracles, alone of all the gods, on the ground that he honoured him so much.
sentences.n: Τῆς δ’ ἐμπεσούσης is a genitive absolute — a noun and participle in the genitive standing loose from the main sentence, setting the circumstances: 'the wagon having fallen in…'. δέον is the same thing in the accusative: the neuter participle of impersonal δεῖ standing absolute, 'it being needful'. Impersonals go into the accusative absolute where ordinary verbs take the genitive. εἱστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι used as a plain past, 'he was standing'.

sentences.t:
Αὐτὸς δ’ ἐπιστὰς εἶπε· « Τῶν τρόχων ἅπτου
καὶ τοὺς βόας κέντριζε, τοῖς θεοῖς δ’ εὔχου,
ὅταν τι ποιῇς καὐτός, ἢ μάτην εὔξῃ. »
sentences.tr:
Autos d' epistas eipe· « Tōn trochōn haptou
kai tous boas kentrize, tois theois d' euchou,
hotan ti poiēis kautos, ē matēn euxēi. »
sentences.l: But he himself, having stood over him, said: « Take hold of the wheels and goad the oxen, and pray to the gods when you are yourself doing something too, or you will pray in vain. »
sentences.i: But Heracles himself appeared beside him and said: « Put your hand to the wheels and goad your oxen; pray to the gods when you are doing something yourself as well, or your prayer will be wasted. »
sentences.n: ἐπιστάς, 'having stood over', is the regular verb for a god or a dream appearing at someone's side. ἅπτου takes the genitive (τῶν τρόχων): 'lay hold of'. καὐτός is καὶ αὐτός run together by crasis; the mark over the alpha is the coronis, which is written like a smooth breathing but is not one. εὔξῃ is future middle, 'you will pray' — the same verb as the imperative εὔχου two words earlier, so the sentence ends on the man's own word turned against him. This fable has no epimythium in Chambry; the god's line is the moral.
